art-01.title: Two Ways of Seeing a Work
explain: **Appreciation** of art is the act of looking at a work and putting into words what you see, think, and feel. You do not need any training in art to do it. However, to go beyond “I like it” or “it is strange,” you need to be able to point to what made you react that way. Two ways of seeing help with this.

- **Formal eye**: looks at what is actually visible in the work, such as lines, colors, shapes, textures, and how things are arranged on the picture plane. These are called **formal elements**.
- **Contextual eye**: looks at the circumstances outside the work, such as who made it, when, where, for what purpose, and with what materials.

The two eyes ask different questions. The formal eye asks “What is here?” and the contextual eye asks “Why was it made this way?” The formal eye can be used right in front of the work. The contextual eye usually requires explanatory text or other sources.

One more thing to remember: whether you like a work is a matter of **taste**, so there is no right answer. But if you explain “why” in terms of form and context, your conversation can connect even with people whose tastes differ.

explain.alt: A square frame with equal sides contains an orange circle at the upper right and a green triangle at the lower left, joined by a gray line. On the right are two boxes labeled “formal eye” and “contextual eye.”

body: Let us read the picture on the left with the formal eye. The orange circle is at the upper right, the green triangle is at the lower left, and a gray line slants between them. It is a composition in which warm and cool colors face each other.

With the contextual eye, we ask different questions. Who might have painted this? When, and for what purpose? Was it made on paper or canvas? This information is not in the picture itself, so it has to be found outside.
The two readings help each other. Look closely with form first, then add reasons from context, and your appreciation becomes deeper.

art-02.title: Line, Shape, Texture, and Value
explain: Let us look at the four visual elements that the formal eye meets first.

- **Line**: the trace left by a moving point. Whether it is straight or curved, bent, thick, or thin changes its impression.
- **Shape**: a flat figure enclosed by lines. There are regular shapes such as squares and circles, and free shapes such as a drop of water.
- **Texture**: the quality of a surface that feels rough or smooth.
- **Value**: the degree of lightness and darkness. The degree of brightness is called **lightness**.

explain.alt: Four panels, each with a single line: a straight line, a curved line, a bent line, and a line that grows gradually thicker.
explain.caption: Four kinds of line (abstract example drawn for this lesson)

explain: A line alone can convey a feeling through its direction. Horizontal lines feel calm, vertical lines feel upright, and slanted lines suggest movement. Bent lines often give a sharp impression, and curved lines a soft one. This is a common tendency, not a rule.

**Texture** comes in two kinds. **Actual texture** is what you feel when you touch a surface with your hand, and **visual texture** is a surface that only looks rough or smooth. The bark of a tree painted on a flat sheet of paper is visual texture.

Light and dark create the sense of solidity. When light comes from one side, that side is bright and the other side is dark. A **shadow** forms behind the object. If you paint in steps from light to dark, a flat circle looks like a round sphere.

Adding a shadow that runs toward the lower right makes the sphere feel as if it rests on a floor. Without any lines, the sphere is drawn only through differences in brightness.

art-03.title: Color
explain:
Color can be described by three properties.
- **Hue**: the kind of color, such as red or blue.
- **Lightness**: how light or dark the color is.
- **Chroma**: how vivid or dull the color is. The more gray is mixed in, the lower the chroma.

A **color wheel** arranges hues in a circle. The figure below is a twelve-color wheel used in the tradition of painting with pigments. The way color wheels are constructed varies, and in other models the pairs may differ slightly.

explain.alt: A ring of twelve colors. Starting from yellow at the top and moving clockwise: tangerine, orange, vermilion, red, purple-red, violet, blue-violet, blue, teal, green, and yellow-green.
explain.caption: Twelve-color wheel (abstract example drawn for this lesson)

explain: Colors that sit exactly opposite each other on the color wheel are called **complementary colors**. Red and green, blue and orange, and yellow and violet are typical pairs. When complementary colors are placed side by side, they tend to make each other look more vivid, so they are used to create strong contrast.

Red, orange, and yellow are called **warm colors**, and blue and teal are called **cool colors**. This division is relative. A green that leans toward yellow looks relatively warm, while a green that leans toward blue looks relatively cool.

explain.alt: The upper strip shows blue changing from a bright color to a dark one in five steps. The lower strip shows vivid blue gradually changing into a muted grayish blue in five steps.
explain.caption: Changes in lightness of the same blue (top) and changes in chroma (bottom)

examples.title: Lightness and Chroma with a Single Blue
body: The upper strip in the picture is the same blue mixed with white or black. The hue stays the same and only the lightness changes. The lower strip is the same blue mixed with gray. The hue is the same, but the vividness, that is, the chroma, changes.

The three properties are independent of one another. There are colors that are light yet muted, and colors that are dark yet vivid. When describing a color, separating the three properties lets you convey “what color it is” more precisely.

art-04.title: Composition and Balance
explain: **Composition** refers to how the elements are placed within the picture. Even if you paint the same objects, their feeling changes greatly depending on where and how large they are placed.

**Balance** is a state in which the picture does not look tilted to one side. There are two main ways.
- **Symmetry**: both sides are the same or mirror-like around a central axis. It gives a stable and orderly feeling.
- **Asymmetrical balance**: the two sides differ, but their weight is equal. A large element can be placed near the center while small ones are placed far away, and balance can still be achieved. Think of a seesaw.

explain.alt: The left frame is symmetrical around a central vertical dotted line, with two orange circles and a green shape. The right frame is asymmetrical, with one large orange circle on the left and two small green rectangles on the right.
explain.caption: Symmetry (left) and asymmetrical balance (right) (abstract examples drawn for this lesson)

explain: The **rule of thirds** divides the picture into three parts horizontally and vertically, and places important things on or near those lines or at their intersections. It is widely used in photography and painting because it creates a sense of room and tension compared with placing things in the exact center. However, it is not a rule that must be followed, but a tool you may try.

explain.alt: A landscape frame divided by two horizontal and two vertical dotted lines. The horizon lies on the lower horizontal dotted line, an orange circle sits at the upper right intersection, and a black bar lies near the left vertical line.
explain.caption: Rule-of-thirds lines and intersections (abstract example drawn for this lesson)

explain: **Visual flow** is also part of composition. The eye first rests on what is large or has strong contrast, and then moves along the direction of lines and shapes. Reading a composition also means following where the eye starts and where it goes.

examples.title: Reading a Landscape with the Rule of Thirds
body: In the landscape, the horizon lies on the lower horizontal dotted line. Because the sky is given a wide area, the picture feels open and refreshing. The orange circle sits at the upper right intersection, and the black bar is near the left vertical line.

The two elements lie in opposite positions, above and below, so the picture does not lean toward one side. In this way, composition is read not as a single element but as the relationships among elements.

art-05.title: Materials and Techniques: An Overview
explain: Different materials make the same form look different. Let us briefly survey five representative ones.

- **Drawing**: making forms with lines and shading in pencil, charcoal, pen, and so on. It is mostly done in a single color.
- **Watercolor**: painted with transparent paints mixed with water. The white of the paper becomes the bright areas, and once applied, a stroke is hard to correct.
- **Oil painting**: painted with pigments bound in oil. It dries slowly, so it is easy to overpaint and revise.
- **Printmaking**: carved or drawn on a plate, then inked and printed. The same image can be made in many copies.
- **Sculpture**: carved away or built up to make a three-dimensional form. It can be seen from many directions.
In drawing, the density of lines controls darkness. Parallel lines are called **hatching**, and lines crossed over one another are called **cross-hatching**. Darkness can also be made with dots.

explain.alt: Three panels: one with parallel lines only (hatching), one with lines crossing each other (cross-hatching), and one with dots that become denser toward the bottom.
explain.caption: Darkness made with lines and dots (abstract example drawn for this lesson)

explain: Printmaking has many kinds. The woodcut, in which wood is carved, is perhaps the most familiar example. In a woodcut, the carved-away parts receive no ink, while the remaining surface takes ink and prints onto the paper.

examples.title: Why Cross-Hatching Looks Darker
body: The middle panel is the first panel with a second set of lines crossed over it. Because the same area of paper now carries more lines, less of the white paper shows, and it looks darker.
Drawing can thus create steps of light and dark through the direction and spacing of lines alone. It carries the lightness of the previous lesson over into lines.

art-06.title: The Broad Currents of Art History
explain: Art has changed in how it is seen and how it is made from one era to the next. Below are only the broadest currents of Western art. East Asian art and the art of many other regions also have long histories of their own, and the boundaries between periods differ from scholar to scholar. So think of this lesson as a single map.

explain.alt: A time line running from left to right: the Renaissance (14th to 16th centuries), the Baroque (17th century), Impressionism (late 19th century), and Cubism (early 20th century).
explain.caption: Order of the broad currents of Western art (a time line drawn for this lesson)

explain:
- **Renaissance**: 14th to 16th centuries, began in Italy. It sought to revive ancient culture and took great interest in depicting the human body and space as they appear in reality. Linear perspective developed.
- **Baroque**: 17th century. Characterized by strong contrasts of light and shadow and dramatic movement.
- **Impressionism**: late 19th century in France. It captured fleeting impressions of color shifting with the light through quick brushwork. Many works were painted outdoors, and the brushstrokes are visible.
- **Cubism**: early 20th century. A single subject was seen from several directions, split into pieces, and reassembled on one surface.

In the twentieth century, **abstract art** also appeared. It makes works without depicting recognizable subjects, using lines, colors, and forms alone. This is the idea that a work can stand on formal elements alone, as in the pictures in this course.

When memorizing the currents, it helps to remember the questions rather than the names. What were they trying to see? How did they paint it? How was it different from the era before? It is a practice of using the formal eye and the contextual eye together.

examples.title: Changes Between the Currents
body: The Renaissance concerned itself with how to depict the world accurately. Impressionism showed in brushwork that the same object looks different depending on the light. Cubism moved toward the idea that the view from one viewpoint is not the whole truth.
Each current was both an answer to and a challenge to the era before. That is why the same objects are depicted so differently across eras.

art-07.title: Value Structure and the Key System
explain: In painting, the most powerful tool for creating three-dimensional solidity and volume on a two-dimensional surface is **value** (명암, 明暗). Where hue stirs emotion and mood, value builds the framework of form and spatial depth through steps of light and dark. Systematizing value from step 1 (pure white) to step 9 (jet black) is called the nine-step value scale.

explain.alt: Five-part diagram of the value structure of a round solid. Highlight (1) is the part directly lit. Halftone (2) is the midtone. Core shadow (3) is the ridge where light and dark meet. Reflected light (4) is light bounced up from the floor. Cast shadow (5) is the shadow the object throws on the floor. Arrows point to each part.

explain:
A regular five-part value structure forms on the surfaces of three-dimensional forms that receive light. Look at the diagram above.
1. **Highlight**: the brightest point, where the light from the source is reflected directly into the viewer's eye.
2. **Halftone (midtone)**: the middle value region where light falls at an angle. The object's own color and texture are most clearly revealed here.
3. **Core shadow**: the darkest edge of the value structure, the ridge where the path of the light ends and darkness begins.
4. **Reflected light**: indirect light bounced off the surrounding floor or walls, gently lighting the lower part within the dark.
5. **Cast shadow**: the shadow formed on the floor when the object blocks the light source.

Within the whole picture, the distribution of value determines a “key system” that governs the mood of the work. A picture composed mainly of high values (steps 7 to 9), in which the whole picture is bright, is called **high-key**. It conveys brightness, lightness, and sanctity. Conversely, a picture composed mainly of dark values (steps 1 to 3) with strong contrast of light and dark is called **low-key**. It creates dramatic tension, mystery, and a sense of the tragic, as in the works of Rembrandt or Caravaggio.

Principle of focal point formation: the human gaze is drawn instinctively to the area in the picture where the brightest and the darkest regions meet directly, the point of maximum contrast. A skilled painter concentrates the greatest value contrast on the face of the main figure or on the key object, thereby commanding the viewer's gaze.

Limits: simply adding strong value does not make a good painting. If reflected light is painted too bright, the mass of the object breaks down and looks flat. If the outline of a shadow is drawn as sharp as a knife cut, the sense of air disappears. The scale of tones must be adjusted with consideration for the strength of the light and its scattering in the air.

examples.title: Rendering the Value of a Sphere, Step by Step
body: Condition: draw a plaster sphere lit by a single white light from 45 degrees at the upper left.
Step 1: On the side opposite the light, set the core shadow ridge, and set an elliptical shadow area on the floor.
Step 2: Leave reflected light at the lower part of the sphere where it touches the floor, and darken the core shadow to build the sense of volume.
Interpretation: Because reflected light exists inside the dark area, the three-dimensional illusion of the spherical surface curving back around is completed.

examples.title: Analysis of a Low-key Lighting Effect
body: Condition: depict a figure holding a single candle in a dark room.
Step 1: Sink more than 80 percent of the picture into deep darkness at steps 1 to 2 (low-key).
Step 2: Give only the outline of the face next to the candle a step-9 highlight, forming an extreme contrast of light and dark (chiaroscuro).
Interpretation: Unnecessary background detail is buried in darkness, and the viewer's emotional immersion is concentrated on the candle and the expression on the face.

art-08.title: Theory of Color Harmony: Munsell's Color System and Itten's Seven Contrasts
explain: Color does not stay merely a sensory stimulus; it operates according to a scientific coordinate system and precise laws of visual contrast. The two representative systems that artists and designers established to control color and weave it into harmony are the color system of the American **Munsell** (Albert Munsell) and the color-contrast theory of **Johannes Itten**, a master of the Bauhaus.

The Munsell color system quantifies color along three coordinate axes in three-dimensional space.
- **Hue** (H, 색상): based on the five principal hues of red (R), yellow (Y), green (G), blue (B), and purple (P), forming a 100-hue color circle.
- **Value** (V, 명도): forms a vertical central axis from pure black (0) to pure white (10).
- **Chroma** (C, 채도): a measure of the purity of color, from vivid to muted, extending outward from the neutral axis (0).
The Munsell solid is not a symmetrical sphere. Because the maximum chroma differs for each hue, it takes an irregular shape called a **color tree**. For example, yellow reaches its highest chroma at high value, while red reaches its highest chroma at medium value.

Johannes Itten compiled the visual-perceptual conflicts and harmonies that arise when colors touch one another into **seven kinds of color contrast**.
1. **Hue contrast**: primary colors clash with each other to give off the strongest and most elemental energy (for example, the three primaries red, yellow, and blue).
2. **Light-dark contrast**: the stark difference between bright and dark.
3. **Warm-cool contrast**: the emotional contrast of temperature between warm colors (orange, red) and cool colors (teal, blue), which creates a sense of advancing and receding in space.
4. **Complementary contrast**: contrast between colors opposite each other on the color wheel (red and green, yellow and purple), which maximizes each other's chroma.
5. **Simultaneous contrast**: the phenomenon in which, on seeing a color, our eyes unconsciously produce an afterimage of its complement, altering the perception of neighboring colors.
6. **Chroma contrast**: the contrast in vividness between pure primaries and colors dulled by mixing with gray.
7. **Area contrast**: the balance of areas needed to match the brightness and intensity of different colors.

According to the area-contrast principle of Goethe and Itten, each color has its own inherent brightness (luminosity). The brightness ratio of yellow : orange : red : green : blue : purple is 9:8:6:6:4:3. To balance visual weight, the area of each color must be in inverse proportion to its brightness. That is, for yellow and purple to balance, the area ratio must be **yellow 1 : purple 3**. Using bright yellow sparingly and spreading dark purple widely achieves a static balance that does not strain the eye.

Limits: color theory depends heavily not only on physical wavelengths but also on the structure of the human retina and cultural memory. The color reproduction ranges (gamuts) of RGB additive mixing on a computer monitor and CMYK subtractive mixing of canvas pigments differ, so distortion in color conversion between digital work and actual painting must always be corrected.

examples.title: Distributing Color by Area Contrast
body: Condition: place yellow (brightness 9) and purple (brightness 3), a strong complementary pair, harmoniously in one picture.
Step 1: The brightness ratio is 9 : 3 = 3 : 1.
Step 2: The area ratio for visual balance is the inverse of the brightness, so it is 1 : 3.

Interpretation: If yellow is used only in 25 percent of the canvas as an accent, and purple tones cover the remaining 75 percent, the two colors cancel each other's glare and reach perfect visual stability.

Interpretation: Colors do not exist independently. They are constantly perceived as transformed within a network of relationships with the surrounding colors.

art-09.title: Perceiving Space: Perspective, Aerial Perspective, and Gestalt Perception
explain: How does the human eye perceive vast three-dimensional space and depth on a flat canvas? Since the Renaissance, Western art has combined geometric **linear perspective** with optical **aerial perspective** to create a perfect illusion of imagined space. In the twentieth century, **Gestalt** psychology of visual perception revealed the psychological laws by which the human brain organizes visual elements not as separate points or lines but as meaningful whole structures.

The basic framework of linear perspective is the **horizon line**, which represents the observer's eye level, and the **vanishing point**, where parallel lines converge.
- **One-point perspective**: when looking straight at the front of an object, the lines converge on a single vanishing point, creating a strong concentration of depth (as in Leonardo da Vinci's The Last Supper).
- **Two-point perspective**: when looking at the corner of a building, the lines converge on two vanishing points on the horizon, giving a majestic sense of solidity.
- **Three-point perspective**: when looking down from above (bird's-eye view) or up from below (worm's-eye view), a third vanishing point is added above or below, producing dramatic spatial distortion.

Linear perspective alone cannot express deep atmosphere. The introduction into painting of the scattering of light by water vapor and dust particles in the air is called **aerial perspective**. The more distant a mountain or background, (1) the more the contrast of light and dark weakens, (2) the detailed outlines are blurred and softened, and (3) warm colors disappear and the scene turns a bluish gray (cool blue) due to Rayleigh scattering.

Four principles of organization in Gestalt visual psychology:
1. **Law of proximity**: elements that are close together are perceived as one group.
2. **Law of similarity**: elements of similar shape, size, or color are seen as related.
3. **Law of continuity**: the eye flows in the direction in which a line or form continues smoothly rather than bending sharply.
4. **Law of closure**: when an outline is incomplete or broken, the brain fills in the missing part on its own and perceives a closed, complete form.

Limits: Renaissance single-point perspective presupposes the artificial assumption of one fixed eye in one place. Real humans shift their gaze constantly with two eyes and synthesize objects in three dimensions. It was this critique of the artificial limits of classical perspective that gave rise to Cézanne's multiple viewpoints and Picasso's Cubism.

examples.title: Creating a Sense of Distance in a Landscape with Aerial Perspective
body: Condition: include in one picture a huge tree in the foreground, a hill village in the middle ground, and a snow-capped mountain in the distance.
Step 1: The tree in the foreground is painted with strong contrast of light and dark, and with clear dark-brown and deep-green detail.
Step 2: The mountain in the distance is reduced to one or two steps of difference between light and dark, its outline softened, and it is painted in a pale bluish-gray tone.
Interpretation: The light-scattering effect of the layers of air visually creates a spatial depth of tens of kilometers.

Interpretation: By omitting detail rather than drawing everything meticulously (inducing closure), the artist draws out the viewer's active participation.

art-10.title: Methods of Art History I: Heinrich Wölfflin's Five Pairs of Concepts
explain: The school that turned the history of art away from listing artists' biographies or interpreting literary content, and toward the “laws of change in visible form,” is the **formalist style history** (Formalism), a true turning point in scholarship. The Swiss art historian **Heinrich Wölfflin** (1864–1945) proposed **five pairs of opposed concepts** in his major work, “Principles of Art History” (1915), to explain the transition from the classical style of the sixteenth-century Renaissance to the Baroque style of the seventeenth century.

explain.alt: Diagram of Heinrich Wölfflin's five pairs of stylistic concepts. The Renaissance classical style on the left and the Baroque dynamic style on the right face each other across five opposed pairs: linear versus painterly, plane versus depth, closed versus open form, multiplicity versus unity, and absolute versus relative clarity.

explain:
Let us decode Wölfflin's five pairs of opposed concepts precisely.
1. **Linear versus painterly**: the Renaissance renders the clear outlines and edges of things tactilely, as if they could be touched like sculpture (Raphael). The Baroque, by contrast, lets outlines dissolve into light and shadow and depicts color and tone fused into one visual flow (Rembrandt).
2. **Plane versus depth**: the Renaissance arranges figures side by side in layers parallel to the picture plane. The Baroque uses diagonal compositions and spiraling movement that draw the viewer's gaze deep into the picture.
3. **Closed form versus open form**: the Renaissance is complete within the frame, closed along vertical and horizontal axes. The Baroque lets the movement or gaze of figures spill beyond the frame, continuous with the space outside.
4. **Multiplicity versus unity**: in the Renaissance, each part keeps its own completeness and the parts combine harmoniously. In the Baroque, the individual parts are absorbed into one dominant light or dynamic movement that governs the whole.
5. **Absolute clarity versus relative clarity**: the Renaissance reveals the original form of every object clearly, without omission. The Baroque reveals only the important parts in a violent play of light and darkness and lets the rest sink into ambiguity.

Wölfflin argued that this change is not a difference in the skill of artists but an evolution of the **“way of seeing”** (Sehform) of humanity. That is, the paradigm of perception shifted from an age that grasped things through line to an age that captured them through light and mass.

Limits: Wölfflin's schema was criticized for trapping stylistic change in an overly mechanical dichotomy. It was faulted for ignoring the “socio-historical context in which the works were produced,” such as the Reformation, the rise of absolute monarchy, class struggle, and iconographic symbolism, and for clinging only to surface appearance (form). These limits were later supplemented by Erwin Panofsky's iconology and Arnold Hauser's social history of art.

examples.title: A Wölfflinian Comparison of Renaissance and Baroque Portraits
body: Condition: compare Raphael's portrait with Rembrandt's self-portrait.

Step 1: In Raphael's portrait, the chin line and the collar of the sitter are closed off by clear lines (linear), and the figure is placed in a stable triangular composition of vertical and horizontal axes (closed form).

Step 2: In Rembrandt's work, only part of the face is lit by rough brushwork and emerging highlights (painterly) against the dark, and the shoulder line dissolves completely into the dark background (relative clarity, unity).
Interpretation: The stylistic break between the two works is fully analyzed as a formal analysis under Wölfflin's five categories.

body: Condition: compare the compositions of Leonardo's and Tintoretto's Last Supper.
Step 1: Leonardo arranges the long table in perfect parallel with the viewer's gaze (plane).
Step 2: Tintoretto thrusts the table diagonally from the lower left of the picture deep into the right (depth), creating a dynamic sense of spatial rush.
Interpretation: This is a typical case in which the flat alignment of the Renaissance passes into the diagonal depth of the Baroque.

art-11.title: Methods of Art History II: Erwin Panofsky's Three Levels of Iconology
explain: The discipline that asks, beyond “What is depicted in the picture?”, “What worldview and ideas of its era does this painting embody?” is **iconology**. The German-born American art historian **Erwin Panofsky** (1892–1968) strictly defined the depth of interpretation in three levels.

explain.alt: Erwin Panofsky's three levels of iconological interpretation. Level 1, pre-iconographical description (natural subject matter, everyday experience); level 2, iconographical analysis (conventional subject matter, knowledge of literature and mythology); and level 3, iconological interpretation (intrinsic meaning, zeitgeist and worldview), linked by arrows pointing downward.

explain:
Let us look at Panofsky's three levels of interpretation.
1. **Level 1: pre-iconographical description**
- Subject: the most elementary **natural subject matter**, meaning the lines, colors, and forms visible on the surface, and the people, animals, trees, and sorrowful or smiling expressions they represent.
- Knowledge required: **practical experience** that everyone has. It can be recognized with the eyes alone, without special reading. Example: “Thirteen men are seated at a table, talking, with bread and wine before them.”

2. **Level 2: iconographical analysis**
- Subject: **conventional subject matter**, culturally agreed upon. The gestures of figures, the attributes they hold, and allegories are connected to a particular story or religious event.
- Knowledge required: **knowledge of literary sources** on the Bible, Greek and Roman mythology, and literary texts. Example: “The central figure at the table is Jesus, the figure clutching a money bag is Judas, and this is the scene of ‘The Last Supper.’”

3. **Level 3: iconological interpretation**
- Subject: the **intrinsic meaning or content** lying at the deepest layer of the work.
- Knowledge required: **historical insight and the spirit of the age** that penetrates the philosophy, religious views, class structure, and psychological attitudes of the period. Example: “Why was this Last Supper produced in fifteenth-century Milan with geometric perspective and classical balance? It expresses the worldview of Renaissance humanism, which departed from medieval mysticism and sought to reconstruct the universe in rational order.”

Panofsky built correction principles into each level so that interpreters do not fall into arbitrary imagination. At the first level, one checks against the history of styles; at the second, against the history of types; and at the third, against the history of cultural symptoms.

Limits: iconology fits perfectly the paintings of antiquity, the Middle Ages, and the Renaissance, which are rich in literary texts (the Bible and mythology). But when interpreting twentieth-century pure abstract painting (Mondrian, Jackson Pollock) or minimalist sculpture, where literary narrative has disappeared, its second level of iconographical analysis does not work, revealing its limits.

examples.title: Three-Level Interpretation of Jan van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait
body: Level 1 (pre-iconographical description): in a room, a woman in a green dress and a man in a fur coat stand holding hands, with a small dog at their feet.

Level 2 (iconographical analysis): the discarded wooden clogs signify a sacred place (the marriage vow), the dog signifies fidelity, and the single candle hanging from the ceiling signifies the presence of God. It is thus an iconographic marriage vow.

Level 3 (iconological interpretation): it is a visual symptom of the worldview of the early capitalist merchant class of fifteenth-century Flanders, which tried to attain sacred religiosity and the display of worldly wealth at the same time.
Interpretation: an ordinary painting of a married couple is elevated, through three levels, into a deep intellectual history of fifteenth-century Flemish society.

body: Condition: a statue of a woman holding a sword and scales, with her eyes covered.
Level 1: the sword, scales, blindfold, and female figure are perceived.

Level 2: from the literature one learns that the scales signify fair judgment, the sword signifies the strict enforcement of law, and the blindfold signifies fairness without prejudice. This is an allegory of the goddess of justice (Dike/Justitia).
Interpretation: prior literary knowledge of attributes is an essential requirement for the second level, iconographical analysis.

art-12.title: Methods of Art History III: Social History of Art and Feminist Criticism
explain: Works of art are not born alone in the head of a solitary genius. They are produced and circulated on a historical ground where money, power, social class, and gender order are intricately entangled. The current that went beyond pure formalism and textual iconology to dig into art as a “social product” is the **social history of art** and **feminist art history**.

1. **Social history of art**: represented by Arnold Hauser and T. J. Clark. They analyze the **economic demands of patrons** hidden behind the forms of works, the institutional controls of guilds and academies, and the art market and class ideology. For example, Renaissance masterpieces were products of the political display of power and the accumulation of capital by the Medici family or the papacy, while Manet's Olympia in the nineteenth century was a visual scandal that starkly exposed the hypocritical sexual exchanges and class contradictions of the Parisian bourgeoisie.

2. **Feminist art history**: ignited in earnest by Linda Nochlin's provocative 1971 essay **“Why Have There Been No Great Women Artists?”**. Nochlin showed that the question itself was wrong. Women did not lack artistic talent compared with men; rather, art academies legally barred women from the nude drawing (human anatomy) classes, and guilds blocked their admission, so that **social institutions and educational opportunities systematically excluded women**.

Visual culture and the “male gaze”: the British critic John Berger, in Ways of Seeing (1972), sharply dismantled the Western nude tradition. “Men act and women appear.” The naked women on canvas did not exist for themselves; they were passive objects displayed for the erotic visual pleasure of the male viewer who would buy the picture.

Limits: social reductionism runs the risk of demoting the aesthetic beauty of works and the original formal achievements of individual artists to mere tools of economic class or ideology. True criticism must capture both formal excellence and its tension with social context.

examples.title: A Social-Historical Analysis of a Renaissance Patron Contract
body: Condition: examine the commission contract for an altarpiece from a fifteenth-century Florentine workshop.
Step 1: The contract specifies, in grams, the amount of ultramarine (a lapis lazuli pigment more expensive than gold) for the Virgin's robes and the weight of pure gold leaf.
Step 2: The painter was not someone who painted by free inspiration, but a skilled artisan who faithfully worked expensive materials to display the patron's wealth.
Interpretation: The style and splendor of an artwork were strongly determined, before any pure artistic will, by the patron's economic contract terms.

examples.title: Analysis of Institutional Exclusion in Nochlin's Critique
body: Condition: investigate the rules on women's education at European royal art academies in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.
Step 1: To paint the highest-status history painting, the study of nude models to understand human musculature was essential.
Step 2: However, the academies, citing “indecency,” completely banned women from the nude studio and permitted only subordinate genres such as still life and landscape.
Interpretation: The absence of women masters was not the result of a lack of individual talent, but of the structural inequality of the academic system.

art-13.title: Turning Points in Art History I: From the Renaissance to Impressionism, Cubism, and Abstraction
explain: The history of Western art is a dramatic paradigm shift. It began with the inquiry “**how should visible nature be represented?**” and moved toward the liberation of “**how to become autonomous through a pure formal language invisible to the eye**.”

1. **Renaissance (15th to 16th centuries)**: established linear perspective, chiaroscuro, and anatomy, making the two-dimensional plane a transparent window onto the world (“Alberti's window”). Perfect proportion and ideal harmony were the absolute standard of beauty.
2. **Impressionism (late nineteenth century)**: in the mid-nineteenth century, the invention of photography and the appearance of tube paints led painters out of the studio into the open air (plein air). To capture the fleeting visual impression of light changing from moment to moment, they placed colors side by side on the canvas instead of mixing them on the palette. Rather than the fixed forms of realism, “the trembling of light and atmosphere” became the protagonist of painting.

3. **Cézanne and Cubism (early twentieth century)**: Paul Cézanne, alarmed by the dissolution of form in Impressionism, urged that nature be seen as spheres, cones, and cylinders. Picasso and Braque, inheriting this, produced **Cubism**, which utterly shattered the single-viewpoint perspective that had ruled Western art for five hundred years. They observed an object from above, below, and the sides at once, broke it into geometric fragments, and recomposed them on a single canvas plane (the coexistence of multiple viewpoints).

4. **Abstract art (from the 1910s)**: they threw off even the last constraint of representing natural subjects such as figures and landscapes. Wassily Kandinsky's “lyrical abstraction” expressed inner spirituality through the resonance of point, line, plane, and color themselves, as music does. Piet Mondrian's “geometric abstraction” built a universal order of the cosmos using only horizontal and vertical lines, the three primary colors (red, yellow, and blue), and achromatic colors.

Limits: the dissolution of representation and the move toward abstraction freed art from literary storytelling, but at the same time produced the elitist isolation of modernism, in which the public found it hard to understand works without difficult art theory and the commentary of critics.

examples.title: The Paradigm Shift Brought by Photography
body: Condition: the commercialization of daguerreotype photography in 1839.
Step 1: In the function of exactly duplicating things, the camera, a machine, became something no human hand could possibly keep up with.

Step 2: Painting handed over the mechanical depiction of appearance to photography and turned toward the inner essence of painting that the camera cannot capture: the subjective impression of light, emotion, and pure color and form.
Interpretation: The challenge of photography was the decisive catalyst that leapt painting from old imitation into modern abstract art.

Interpretation: It is an innovative visual language that condenses on a two-dimensional plane the temporality of human perception, which observes an object by looking around it over time.

art-14.title: Turning Points in Art History II: Avant-garde, Conceptual Art, and Beyond Genre
explain: The most radical event in twentieth-century contemporary art was the upheaval of the question itself: **“What is art?”** Art moved from “the art of the skilled hand,” which made beautiful objects through manual craft, to **“the art of thinking,”** which poses questions to the world and overturns contexts.

1. **Marcel Duchamp and the Ready-made**: in 1917 Duchamp turned a mass-produced men's urinal on its back, signed it with a pseudonym (R. Mutt), and submitted it to an exhibition under the title “Fountain.” This provocation fundamentally overturned the definition of art. He declared that the essence of art lies not in whether the artist carved and painted the work by hand, but in the **conceptual choice** of placing everyday objects in a new context to produce new thought.

2. **Conceptual art (1960s)**: Joseph Kosuth's “One and Three Chairs” (1965) displayed an actual wooden chair, a photograph of that chair, and the dictionary definition of “chair” side by side. Kosuth declared that the work as a physical object is secondary, and that **“the idea and concept itself is the true art.”**

3. **Minimalism and spatial presence**: Donald Judd, Robert Morris, and others placed industrial iron plates and aluminum boxes, stripped of all emotional expression, casually on the gallery floor. Erasing the mystery of the work itself, they created a theatrical situation in which the viewer perceives their own bodily presence within the space and light surrounding the work.

4. **Installation art and relational aesthetics**: contemporary art has broken out of frames and pedestals into the entire exhibition space, and further into open land (Earth Art) and cities. The French critic Nicolas Bourriaud understood art since the 1990s as a “device that catalyzes social relations,” one that communicates with viewers and forms communities (for example, the work of Rirkrit Tiravanija, who cooks pad thai for visitors in the gallery).

Limits: the dematerialization in which physical works disappear and only ideas remain made art extremely intellectual, like a philosophy paper or a linguistic puzzle, deepening its distance from general audiences. Paradoxically, the concepts themselves were then traded at high prices in commercial galleries, facing the limits of capitalist absorption.

Interpretation: The artist's role changed from a physical “maker” to a conceptual “namer” who redefines meaning.

art-15.title: Theory of East Asian Painting: Six Principles, Spirit Resonance, Expressive Intent, and Blank Space
explain: Whereas Western art reproduced the outward appearance of external objects objectively through mathematical perspective and chiaroscuro, traditional East Asian painting took as its lifelong question: **“how should the cosmic life force dwelling beyond the appearance of things, and the inner spirit of the painter, be contained?”**

The one who set the lasting standard of East Asian painting criticism is **Xie He** (사혁, 謝赫), a painter and critic of the Southern Qi during the Northern and Southern Dynasties of the fifth century. In the preface to his work Gu Hua Pin Lu (고화품록, 古畫品錄), he declared the **six principles** (육법, 六法) for judging a good painting.
1. **Spirit resonance and vitality** (기운생동, 氣韻生動): the cosmic life force and the breath of qi should vividly stir throughout the whole picture. This is the foremost of the six principles and its highest realm.
2. **Brushwork with bone structure** (골법용필, 骨法用筆): the brushstroke should carry skeletal structure and vigorous force.
3. **Responding to things in forming their shapes** (응물상형, 應物象形): depict the form of the subject appropriately.
4. **Applying color according to kind** (수류부채, 隨類賦彩): apply colors suited to the nature of each thing.
5. **Planning composition and placement** (경영위치, 經營位置): consider layout and placement deeply to achieve harmony.
6. **Transmitting through copying** (전이모사, 傳移模寫): copy and master the models of the great old masters so that their methods are inherited.

Literati painting (문인화, 文人畫) and the spirit of **sa-ui** (사의, 寫意): from the Song and Ming dynasties onward, the literati painting tradition, produced by poets and scholars, blossomed in opposition to the technique-centered painting of professional court painters. They regarded the mere copying of outward appearance, hyeongsa (형사, 形似), as vulgar, and aspired to **“sa-ui” (사의, 寫意, painting the intention)**, pouring the painter's noble character and purpose onto the tip of the brush. Su Dongpo exclaimed that “if one discusses painting only in terms of resemblance of form, that discernment is no better than a child's.”

**Aesthetics of empty space** (여백, 餘白): the white paper left unpainted in East Asian landscape painting is not mere incompleteness. It is the ever-changing clouds, mist, and waves, and the full ontological space of the Laozi and Zhuangzi (노장, 老莊) idea that “being is born from non-being.” Whereas Western blank space is a background to be painted, East Asian blank space breathes as an invisible reality with weight equal to the lines of ink.

Unity of poetry, calligraphy, and painting (시·서·화 일치, 詩書畫一致): within a single picture, the literary poem (詩), the calligraphic brushwork (書), and the pictorial form (畫) melt into one, and the painter's seal (落款) completes the totality of visual art and the humanities.

examples.title: Comparing “Spirit Resonance” and “Formal Likeness” in the Six Principles
body: Condition: compare two painters' approaches to painting a pine tree.
Step 1: Painter A rendered each pine needle and the pattern of the bark exactly like a photograph, but the result is stiff and lacks life (succeeded in formal likeness, failed in spirit resonance).

Step 2: The literati painter B hurried through the twisting trunk with a few thick, rough dry-brush (갈필) strokes. Yet the pine rising through a crevice of rock keeps its unyielding life force and spirit, keenly alive (achievement of spirit resonance).
Interpretation: The value of East Asian painting lies not in the precise replication of outward appearance but in the vitality of qi.

Step 2: The large unpainted blank becomes a broad lake and thick morning mist, conveying an infinite sense of space.
Interpretation: The essence of East Asian aesthetics is completing fullness (有) through emptiness (無).

art-16.title: Medium Aesthetics: From the Materiality of Paint to New Media Art
explain: When facing a work of art, we tend to focus only on the “content” of the picture. But the history of art has always been led by **medium and the materiality of materials**. Which pigment and binder are used, and whether the support is canvas, iron plate, or a video screen, completely changes the visual texture and the aesthetic impact that is conveyed.

1. **Evolution of painting materials**: medieval **tempera** used egg yolk as its binder, drying quickly and suited to precise, flat linework. **Oil paint**, which flowered in fifteenth-century Flanders, used linseed oil as its binder, so it dried very slowly. Because of this slow drying, it was possible to soften brushmarks with sfumato and to layer transparent glazes (glazing), creating a jewel-like luster and realistic skin textures. The **acrylic paint** of the twentieth century is a synthetic resin that dissolves in water but becomes water-resistant when dry, giving modern painters immediate drying and intense flat, pure colors.

2. **Materiality and space of sculpture**: sculpture divides into subtractive carving (marble, wood), which removes mass, and additive modeling (clay, bronze casting), which builds up material. Since Rodin, modern sculpture evolved toward revealing the grain of wood and the metallic luster of the material itself, as in the work of Brancusi. Andy Warhol's “Brillo Box” broke down the material boundary between artworks and the cardboard boxes of the supermarket.

3. **Nam June Paik and video and new media art**: in the 1960s, Paik distorted the internal coils of TV monitors with magnets, using electromagnetic signals themselves as the canvas of art. Video art brought into the medium of painting **temporality and “electronic signals of moving light,”** beyond the fixed materials of painting and sculpture. Today, interactive media art and AI generative art use the viewer's bodily responses and algorithmic code as new aesthetic materials.

Clement Greenberg's medium specificity: the modernist critic Greenberg insisted that painting should not imitate literature or theater, but remain faithful only to the limits of its own medium, the “flatness” of the canvas cloth and the materiality of paint.

Limits: if one clings too much to medium specificity, art is trapped in the formal blind spot of materialism. Under the contemporary “post-medium” condition, painting, installation, performance, and virtual reality (VR) merge without boundaries, so emphasis should be placed on the spatial and critical experiences they create rather than on the material constraints of the medium.

Step 2: Light passes through the transparent layers of paint, reflects off the ground, and emerges again, radiating a deep, luminous glow.
Interpretation: The physical property of oil paint, which dries slowly, made possible the deep skin and fabric textures of classic masterpieces.

Step 2: The TV, once a passive receiving device, is transformed by the artist's intervention into an active electronic abstract canvas.
Interpretation: It is the origin of new media art, which artistically disrupted and hacked the one-way communication structure of the medium.

art-17.title: Exhibition Planning (Curating): White Cube, Circulation, and the Staging of the Gaze
explain: Once an artwork leaves the studio and hangs in an **exhibition space**, it becomes part of the narrative and spatial environment staged by the curator. Exhibition planning, which designs “on which wall, at what height, in what order, and under what lighting” a work is shown, is another creative act that gives the works new life and interpretation.

explain.alt: Plan of exhibition circulation and gaze guidance. Starting from the entrance on the left, the route passes 1 introduction (wall text), 2 development (representative work A), turns around the central partition to 3 climax (key work B, spot-lit), then 4 epilogue (archive), and leads to the exit on the right along a curved dotted route.

explain: 1. **White cube: its aesthetics and limits**: the white walls, colorless floor, and artificially lit space without natural light that became the standard of museums in the twentieth century. It isolates works from the noise and context of the outside world, making them objects of absolute reverence beyond space and time. However, as Brian O'Doherty criticized in “Inside the White Cube,” the white cube is never a neutral space. It is also an institutional and ideological space that maximizes the commodity value of the bourgeois art market.

2. **Circulation and narrative construction**: look at the diagram above. An exhibition must have a narrative breath, like a film or a novel.
- **Introduction**: near the entrance, a large wall text (the exhibition preface) and an artist's note evoke the problem consciousness of the exhibition.
- **Development**: the central partition divides the space so that visitors cannot see all the works at once, and tension rises gradually as they move.
- **Climax**: the deepest, central point where the gazes converge holds the exhibition's core masterpiece (representative work B) alone, given a strong visual aura by a focused spotlight.
- **Epilogue**: near the exit, the artist's drawings, interview videos, and archival materials extend reflection and leave a lingering aftertaste.

3. **Engineering standards of display**: the international eye-level standard places the center line of a painting at **145 to 150 cm above the floor**, the average eye level of an adult. Keep at least 50 to 100 cm between works to avoid visual interference. To prevent glare and reflection on the surface of works, lighting is aimed from the wall at a 30-degree angle, and the color temperature is kept at a natural warm white (3000 to 4000 K).

Limits: a one-way layout that forces a uniform route on visitors can restrict their free, subjective appreciation. Contemporary curating actively introduces multi-directional network circulation, in which visitors choose their own paths and explore the space, and interactive spatial staging.

examples.title: Exhibition Lighting Angle and Glare Prevention
body: Condition: install spotlights for an oil painting in a glass frame.
Step 1: If the light falls vertically (90 degrees) from directly above the ceiling, the viewer's head shadow falls on the work.
Step 2: Adjusting track lights to a 30-degree angle of incidence relative to the wall sends the light reflected by the glass down to the floor, completely preventing viewer glare.
Interpretation: The angle and color temperature of the lighting determine the quality of appreciation, and they are the technical fundamentals of curating.

Step 2: For the center line of the work to be at 150 cm above the floor, the floor height of the bottom edge must be $150 - 60 = 90$ cm.
Interpretation: Even if works differ in size, aligning each center line with the 150 cm horizon gives the entire wall a graceful visual stability.

art-18.title: Conservation Science and Connoisseurship: Climate Control and the Principle of Reversibility
explain: Famous paintings from centuries ago can still exist before our eyes without losing their brilliance, thanks to **conservation science**, the art of preserving art out of sight. Where restoration in the past was “artistic repair” that imitated the painter's brushwork by overpainting, modern conservation science is a precise scientific intervention that integrates physics, chemistry, and microbiology to extend the life of works.

1. **Environmental control: the first principle of conservation**: about 90 percent of damage to artworks originates in an inappropriate environment. The most damaging factor is a sudden fluctuation of temperature and humidity. Canvas and wood panels expand when they absorb moisture and contract when they dry. The oil paint layers on them have no elasticity, so when temperature and humidity swing, the paint layer cracks like a spider's web, called **crackle**, and eventually flakes away (flaking, 박락). Therefore storerooms and galleries must be kept constant, 24 hours a day, at **20 ± 2 °C temperature and 50 ± 5% relative humidity**. Ultraviolet (UV) light also destroys the molecular bonds of pigments and causes fading, so it must be fully blocked to 75 μW/lumen or below.

2. **The three ethical principles of conservation and restoration**:
- **Principle of reversibility**: every synthetic resin, adhesive, and inpainting material used in conservation must be a **substance that future conservators can remove completely, in 50 or 100 years, without damaging the original**. The use of an adhesive that bonds permanently to the original and cannot be removed (for example, epoxy) is absolutely forbidden.
- **Minimal intervention**: intervene only in the smallest area where damage has occurred, in order to preserve the original creator's hand.
- **Discernibility**: the damaged areas filled by the conservator look natural to the ordinary viewer's eye, but when a specialist examines them closely with a magnifier or a UV lamp, the artist's original brushwork and the conservator's inpainting brushwork must be clearly distinguishable (to prevent forgery).

3. **Scientific diagnostic techniques for connoisseurship**:
- **X-ray fluorescence (XRF)**: without damaging the work, identifies within a second the chemical elements in the paint (lead, cadmium, titanium, and others). If titanium white pigment, which was invented in 1920, is detected in a seventeenth-century masterpiece, the work is a 100 percent forgery.
- **Infrared reflectography (IRR)**: infrared passes through the oil paint layer and is absorbed by the graphite underdrawing beneath, revealing every underdrawing the painter hid beneath the paint and the traces of changes in composition (pentimento).
- **Ultraviolet fluorescence (UV)**: aged varnish fluoresces, while recent overpainting and inpainted areas absorb the light and appear dark, exposing the traces of past restorations.

Limits: conservation science can slow physical aging, but it cannot turn time back. Excessive cleaning (over-cleaning) that tries to make a work shine like new can permanently destroy the artist's delicate final glaze layers. It must therefore be accompanied by a philosophical consensus on how far the patina (고색, 古色) left by the years should be accepted.

examples.title: Detecting a Forgery Through Non-destructive Elemental Analysis by XRF
body: Condition: an oil painting, claimed to be an unknown authentic work by the seventeenth-century Dutch master Vermeer, has been submitted for appraisal.
Step 1: When the white paint was analyzed by XRF, a strong titanium dioxide (TiO₂) peak was detected.
Step 2: Titanium white pigment is a modern material first commercialized in 1921. Seventeenth-century Vermeer used only lead white (lead).
Interpretation: Through material analysis, it was scientifically demonstrated that this was an elaborate forgery produced after the twentieth century.

examples.title: Practicing the Principle of Reversibility
body: Condition: reinforce the back of a torn eighteenth-century canvas.
Step 1: In the past, permanent adhesives were used to stiffen the canvas, causing secondary damage.
Step 2: Modern conservators use natural animal glue or a special reversible synthetic resin (Beva 371) that can later be washed out with warm water or a mild solvent without harming the original.
Interpretation: Conservation ethics means leaving the path open, so that earlier treatments can be reversed whenever better technology emerges in future generations.

Therefore, a specialist examining it closely must be able to clearly identify where the original artist's hand ends and where the later conservator's intervention begins, so that academic and ethical honesty is preserved.

art-19.title: Bachelor's Capstone: Integrated Criticism of Form, Iconography, and Social History
explain: The pinnacle of the bachelor's program in art is to bring together **formal principles (value, color, perspective), art-historical methods (Wölfflin's five pairs, Panofsky's three levels of iconological interpretation, and social-historical criticism), and medium aesthetics and conservation science** in the criticism of a single work, producing a multilayered and three-dimensional critical essay.

Let us take the hypothetical painting <Dawn Oath> (새벽의 서약), a seventeenth-century Baroque oil painting, oil on canvas, 180 × 240 cm, as the object of criticism.
1. **Formal and compositional analysis**: applying Wölfflin's framework, the outlines of the figures dissolve into darkness, which is painterly. The strong diagonal running from the candle to the window at the back is depth. The figure gazing beyond the frame is open form. The whole is integrated into a single chiaroscuro contrast, showing single unity and relative clarity.
2. **Iconological analysis**: at Level 1 of Panofsky's method, one identifies an old man in a black robe, a young man holding a knife, and a broken hourglass on the table. At Level 2, the broken hourglass is confirmed from the literature as an allegory of vanitas (Vanitas, “all is vanity”), the symbol of the transience of human life. At Level 3, this is a sign of the existential worldview of the seventeenth-century northern European middle class, who tried to overcome the fear of death through religious resolve amid the devastation of the Thirty Years' War.
3. **Medium and conservation diagnosis**: the chiaroscuro depth was achieved through glazing in oil paint, but because of improper temperature and humidity control, fine network crackle appeared at the upper right of the picture. XRF analysis confirmed the natural smalt (cobalt) blue pigment of the period, and it was judged that, in restoration, the paint should be inpainted with reversible varnish and synthetic resin.

Good art criticism is born when a precise sensitivity to surface (form), an intellectual tracing of the inner meaning through the texts (iconography), and insight into the zeitgeist that produced the work (social history) are interlocked as a trinity.

Limits: the critic must guard against anachronism, that is, forcing one's own subjective feelings or modern prejudices onto works of the past. Every sentence of criticism must be anchored in concrete visual evidence from the work and in historical sources.

examples.title: Structure of a Multilayered Art Critique
body: Step 1 (form): argue the low-key chiaroscuro and the painterly, open, diagonal composition in Wölfflin's terms.
Step 2 (iconography): establish the vanitas iconography from the hourglass and skull attributes, through literary sources.
Step 3 (society and worldview): connect it with the Calvinist ethics of seventeenth-century Netherlands, where war and plague swept the land.
Interpretation: Form, iconography, and social history converge into one completed critical narrative without being separated.

examples.title: Critique Combined with Conservation Diagnosis
body: Condition: a critique of the conservation state of a picture in which crackle has occurred.
Step 1: Diagnose the damage from the expansion and contraction of the canvas caused by temperature and humidity fluctuations.
Step 2: Propose a cleaning and inpainting plan premised on the principle of reversibility.
Interpretation: Diagnosis of the material life of the work, undertaken to permanently protect its historical value, is also brought into the domain of criticism.

art-20.title: Bachelor's Capstone: Curatorial Proposal for a Thematic Exhibition and Critical Essay
explain: The final capstone task of the bachelor's program is to write, for an imaginary museum or gallery, a **curatorial exhibition proposal and critical essay on representative works**, and to review it rigorously. Beyond viewing artworks one at a time, you complete a practical plan like that of a professional curator: you build the thematic narrative of the exhibition, select three representative works and critique them formally and iconographically, and fully plan the circulation, lighting, and conservation measures.

The standard seven-part framework of the proposal is as follows.
1. **Exhibition overview and planning intent**: exhibition title, background of the planning, the contemporary question posed to viewers, and the curatorial narrative
2. **Space and circulation design**: floor-plan partitions of the white cube space, circulation along the introduction, development, climax, and epilogue sequence, and the gaze-guidance strategy
3. **Composition of works**: reasons for selecting the three core representative works and their placement (recommended: one original painting, one sculpture or installation, and one new media or archive work)
4. **Critique of works (form and iconography)**: Wölfflin-style formal analysis and three-level Panofskyan iconological criticism of the representative works
5. **Display and lighting engineering**: the eye-level installation standard (145–150 cm), spacing between works, 30-degree track spotlights to prevent glare, and the design of color temperature (K)
6. **Conservation science and safety management**: control of exhibition temperature and humidity (20 °C, 50%), UV blocking, handling of fragile works on the principle of reversibility, and a condition-report plan
7. **Critical self-evaluation**: the novelty of the planning, anticipated limits, and supplementary points on communication with the audience and accessibility (barrier-free)

A successful proposal has its space and narrative tightly **synchronized**. The wall text opens the viewer's curiosity, the brightness of the lighting and the bends of the partitions tune the tension, and the emotional catharsis should burst out in front of the final masterpiece.

In self-evaluation, three questions must be asked. (1) Is my exhibition merely a fair that lines up works, or a meaningful grouping that creates a new discourse? (2) Does the circulation design fatigue visitors or create bottlenecks? (3) Has physical and informational accessibility (barrier-free) been considered for visually impaired people and wheelchair users?

Limits: this capstone task is not automatically graded. Using the provided checklist, the learner compares and supplements their own exhibition proposal rigorously from the standpoint of a curator. All planning must be imaginary, and it must not infringe anyone's copyright.

examples.title: Opening Example of a Proposal for the Exhibition “At the Boundary of Light and Darkness”
body: Exhibition title: “Boundary of Light and Darkness: From Classical Baroque to Contemporary Media Art”

Planning intent: explores a genealogy of light that transcends eras, tracing how seventeenth-century chiaroscuro is reborn in the neon signs of the contemporary city and in interactive media art as “the light of human alienation and salvation.”

Spatial staging: after passing through a dark tunnel at the introduction, visitors meet, in the climax zone, a large oil painting illuminated by a single focused spot. The epilogue connects to an interactive media installation that responds to visitors' movements.
Interpretation: The tension between a clear narrative and spatial circulation maximizes the immersion of the exhibition.

examples.title: Example of Self-critical Review
body: Condition: self-evaluation of the exhibition plan above.
Step 1: Dark lighting staging heightens immersion, but it may endanger the walking safety of visitors with low vision or wheelchair users.
Step 2: Install floor-guide LED indirect lighting, and introduce an audio docent and tactile reproductions to supplement barrier-free accessibility.
Interpretation: This enhances the social responsibility and completeness of the work of a public museum curator.

Through Wölfflin's painterly style and Panofsky's iconology, it criticizes the vanitas symbolism of the representative works, and it guides the gaze with a 150 cm eye level and 30-degree track lighting.
